theme: Controversies; the greatest commandment; woes to scribes
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 22:15-23:39. The leaders test Jesus with questions about taxes, the resurrection, and the greatest commandment. Then Jesus turns the tables and pronounces seven woes on the scribes and Pharisees. Read 22:34-40 slowly.
settingTheScene: The final week in the temple courts is a series of tests. First the Pharisees and Herodians ask about taxes to Caesar, then the Sadducees ask about the resurrection, and then a lawyer asks about the greatest commandment. Jesus answers all of them with wisdom. Then he asks the question that silences his opponents, and he turns to the crowds and disciples to warn them about the hypocrisy of their leaders.
observation: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (22:21).
“You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God” (22:29).
“He is not God of the dead, but of the living” (22:32).
“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind” (22:37).
“On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets” (22:40).
“The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (22:44).
“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (23:12).
interpretation:
Jesus answers the question about taxes with wisdom. The coin bears Caesar’s image, so give it to Caesar. But humans bear God’s image, so give yourselves to God. The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, bring a trick question, and Jesus answers from the Scriptures they accept: God said, “I am the God of Abraham,” and he is the God of the living. The resurrection is rooted in who God is.

The lawyer asks which commandment is the greatest. Jesus gives two: love God with everything, and love your neighbor as yourself. All the law and the prophets hang on these. This is not a replacement for the law but its summary. The whole of the Old Testament is about love of God and neighbor.

Then Jesus asks his question about Psalm 110. If the Christ is David’s son, how does David call him Lord? No one could answer, and from that day, no one dared to ask him any more questions. The Messiah is both human and divine.

Chapter 23 is the most severe passage in the Gospels. Jesus warns the crowds and his disciples about the scribes and Pharisees. They sit on Moses’ seat, so their teaching from Scripture should be heeded, but their practice should not be imitated. They love honor, burden people with rules, and neglect justice, mercy, and faithfulness. “Woe to you, hypocrites!” occurs again and again. They clean the outside of the cup and are full of greed inside. They are whitewashed tombs.

Yet the chapter ends with sorrow, not just anger: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem… How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” The judgment comes from a broken heart. Even so, he promises that they will say, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”
connection: Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18 are the two commandments quoted. Exodus 3:6 is quoted about the God of the living. Psalm 110:1 is the psalm you read on Day 587. Micah 6:8 sums up justice, kindness, and walking humbly. Romans 13:8-10 says love is the fulfilling of the law. 1 John 4:19-21: we love because he first loved us. Luke 13:34-35 has the lament over Jerusalem. Philippians 2:3.
application:
Practice the two great commandments today: choose one concrete act of love for God and one for a neighbor.

Check yourself for hypocrisy: where do you say one thing and do another?

Remember that Jesus grieves over those who refuse him. Pray for someone who resists the gospel.
prayerPrompts: Ask Jesus to teach you to love God with all your heart, soul, and mind.
Ask him to help you love a specific neighbor.
Ask him to keep you from the hypocrisy he warns about.
